title: The Room That Was Measured
topic: clair patterson, the age of the earth, and lead
paragraphs: The age of the Earth is a number most people have heard and almost no one can trace.
It is about 4.55 billion years, published in 1956 by Clair Patterson, a geochemist at the California Institute of Technology then in his early thirties.

What makes the story worth telling is not the number but the obstacle in its way: lead, the element Patterson needed to measure, turned out to be smeared over everything he touched, and clearing it away changed his career and eventually the air of the whole country.
Before radioactivity was understood, the best physics gave a much younger planet.

In the nineteenth century Lord Kelvin treated the Earth as a cooling ball of once-molten rock and concluded from the heat still leaking out of the ground that it could be at most a few tens of millions of years old.
Radioactivity, discovered in 1896, undid that argument twice over: decaying uranium and thorium in the crust supply heat Kelvin had not known about, and they also offer a clock.
Uranium-238 decays to lead-206 with a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, and uranium-235 to lead-207 with one of about 700 million.
Lead-204, by contrast, is produced by no decay at all, so it serves as a fixed reference against which the growing radiogenic isotopes, the ones born of decay, can be measured.
The clock has a catch.

To read a rock's age from its lead you must know how much of each isotope was there at the start, and the Earth's surface rocks have been melted, mixed, and reworked so many times that their starting lead is lost.
Patterson's doctoral adviser at the University of Chicago, Harrison Brown, saw a way around this.
Meteorites are leftovers from the formation of the solar system, and if the Earth formed at the same time, their primordial lead should be the Earth's as well.
Iron meteorites in particular contain almost no uranium, so whatever lead they hold has sat unchanged since they solidified.
The job proved far harder than anyone expected.
Patterson had learned mass spectrometry at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, during the Manhattan Project, and the instrument was not the difficulty.

It appeared when he and a fellow student, George Tilton, measured traces of uranium and lead in zircon crystals from a granite: the uranium numbers were steady, but the lead came out wildly high and different on every run.
A sample might hold only billionths of a gram of lead, and the laboratory was adding more than that from the air, the dust, the paint, the plumbing solder, and the bottled acids themselves.
Patterson was not measuring the rock.
He was measuring the room.
His answer was a laboratory cleaner than any yet built.

At Chicago and then at Caltech, where he moved in 1952, he sealed the walls, boiled his glassware in acid, redistilled his water and reagents in quartz vessels, kept the air in the room at a slightly higher pressure than the hallway, and required everyone who entered to change into clean garments.
Above all he measured the blank: a run through the whole procedure with no sample at all, which reveals how much lead the method itself contributes.
It was slow, unglamorous work, and I think it was the most important thing he ever did, because every measurement that followed rested on it.

Patterson's primordial lead came from the Canyon Diablo meteorite, the iron mass that dug Meteor Crater in Arizona, which he compared with stony meteorites that did contain uranium and so had been accumulating radiogenic lead since they formed.
Plotted as lead-207 against lead-206, each relative to lead-204, the samples fell on a straight line, an isochron, whose slope depends only on the time since they shared the same starting lead.
The slope gave 4.55 billion years, give or take about 70 million, and the value accepted today, about 4.54 billion, sits inside that range.
Lead from modern ocean sediment, standing in for the Earth as a whole, fell on the same line, which meant the planet and the meteorites were the same age.
Patterson spent his next two decades asking where all that lead had come from.
The largest single source was gasoline.
In 1921 Thomas Midgley Jr., a chemist at General Motors, found that a small dose of tetraethyl lead stopped engines from knocking, and the additive went on sale in 1923.
To keep lead from fouling the engine, refiners also blended in halogen compounds that carried it out of the tailpipe as fine particles.

After refinery workers died of lead poisoning in 1924, the Surgeon General called a conference and sales paused, but a brief study found no evidence of public harm and the additive returned to the market in 1926.

In the early 1960s he and his collaborators found far more lead in surface seawater than in the deep water beneath it, a pattern that pointed to recent fallout from the air rather than to any natural source from below.

Greenland snow, which preserves each year's atmosphere, told the same story in 1969: lead in the ice had risen roughly two-hundredfold from the oldest layers to the mid-1960s, most of it after leaded gasoline entered wide use.

In a 1965 paper, 'Contaminated and Natural Lead Environments of Man,' he drew the conclusion that mattered: the amount of lead in a typical modern body was not the natural amount but something like a hundred times higher, and calling it normal confused what is common with what is safe.
For four decades the established view belonged to Robert Kehoe, a physician whose laboratory at the University of Cincinnati was funded largely by the makers of the additive.

Kehoe held that lead was natural in the environment, that the body excreted what it absorbed, and that below a threshold it did no harm, and he could point to thousands of measurements showing that ordinary people carried lead without obvious illness.
Patterson's reply was that every one of those measurements had been compared against the wrong baseline, since the 'normal' people were themselves contaminated.
He said so to a Senate subcommittee under Edmund Muskie in 1966.

It is tempting to tell what followed as one stubborn man against an industry, and I resist that telling only partly: the man was stubborn and the industry was powerful, but the laws that changed were written by other hands and rested on other evidence too.
The Clean Air Act of 1970 gave the new Environmental Protection Agency authority over fuel additives, and in 1973 the agency ordered a gradual reduction of lead in gasoline.
From the 1975 model year, new cars carried catalytic converters, and because lead ruins a catalyst, those cars required unleaded fuel.

In 1979 the pediatrician Herbert Needleman reported that children with more lead in their shed baby teeth scored lower on tests of intelligence and attention, harm at levels Kehoe's threshold had called safe.
In 1985 the agency cut the lead allowed in gasoline by roughly ninety percent, and under amendments passed in 1990 the sale of leaded gasoline for road vehicles ended on the first day of 1996.
Patterson died in December 1995, a few weeks before the ban took full effect.
Patterson's two careers used one tool.

The same discipline that let him trust a few billionths of a gram of lead from a meteorite let him see the lead in seawater, in Greenland snow, and in canned tuna, where most of the metal, he showed in 1980, came from the solder.
A measurement is only as good as its blank, and a judgment about what is normal is only as good as the baseline it is compared to.
I do not think the second lesson has been fully learned.

Lead left gasoline, paint, and solder, but each generation inherits an altered world and calls it natural, and the hard part, as Patterson found, is not the instrument but the willingness to measure what everyone else has agreed to assume.

questions.stem: The author discusses Lord Kelvin in paragraph 2 primarily to
choices: show that nineteenth-century physicists ignored the heat escaping from the ground
contrast an older estimate with the clock that radioactivity made possible
argue that Kelvin's method was sound and only his data were wrong
explain why Patterson chose meteorites rather than rocks from the Earth's surface
demonstrate that the Earth has been cooling steadily since it formed

proof.quote: Before radioactivity was understood, the best physics gave a much younger planet.
undid that argument twice over

questions.why: Paragraph 2 opens by saying the best physics before radioactivity gave a much younger planet, then shows how radioactivity undid Kelvin's argument and offered a clock. Kelvin is there as the before picture that the uranium clock replaces.
distractorNotes: Reversed: Kelvin built his estimate on the heat leaking from the ground; he did not ignore it.
Outside the passage: the author never defends Kelvin's method, and the problem was a missing heat source, not bad data.
Wrong paragraph: the choice of meteorites is explained in paragraph 3, and Kelvin has nothing to do with it.
This is Kelvin's own assumption, not the author's purpose, and paragraph 2 says radioactive decay adds heat he did not know about.

questions.stem: According to the passage, lead-204 is useful as a reference isotope because it
choices: has the longest half-life of any isotope of lead
is the final product of the decay of uranium-235
is found only in iron meteorites and not in Earth rocks
is not created by the decay of any other element
accumulates at a fixed rate as uranium decays

proof.quote: Lead-204, by contrast, is produced by no decay at all, so it serves as a fixed reference

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says lead-204 is produced by no decay at all, which is exactly why it can serve as a fixed reference while the radiogenic isotopes grow.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: no half-life is given for any lead isotope, and lead-204 is described as stable, not decaying.
Wrong isotope: paragraph 2 says uranium-235 decays to lead-207.
Outside the passage: lead-204 is used as a reference in every sample, including Earth sediment in paragraph 6.
Reversed: the isotopes that accumulate as uranium decays are lead-206 and lead-207, not lead-204.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if the Earth's surface rocks had never been melted and reworked, Patterson would most likely have
choices: been able to find the starting lead in rocks from the Earth itself
found that uranium-238 decays more slowly than it does in meteorites
still needed iron meteorites, since Earth rocks contain no lead-204
measured an age for the Earth considerably greater than 4.55 billion years
avoided the contamination that plagued his zircon measurements

proof.quote: the Earth's surface rocks have been melted, mixed, and reworked so many times that their starting lead is lost
their primordial lead should be the Earth's as well

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says the starting lead is lost precisely because surface rocks have been melted, mixed, and reworked, and that meteorites are the way around this. Remove the reworking and the reason for going to meteorites disappears.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: a half-life is a fixed property of the isotope; nothing suggests it differs by location.
Contradicted: paragraph 6 uses lead-204 ratios for Earth sediment, so Earth rocks do contain it.
Unsupported: the passage gives no reason the age itself would change; only the route to the starting lead would.
Wrong paragraph: the contamination in paragraph 4 came from the laboratory, not from the history of the rocks.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when Patterson and Tilton measured zircon crystals as students, they found that
choices: the uranium readings varied wildly while the lead readings stayed steady
the crystals held far less lead than the uranium clock predicted
the mass spectrometer itself was adding lead to every sample
the granite had been melted and reworked so its starting lead was lost
the lead readings were too high and changed from one run to the next

proof.quote: the uranium numbers were steady, but the lead came out wildly high and different on every run

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says the uranium numbers were steady but the lead came out wildly high and different on every run, which is what revealed the contamination.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 4 says the uranium was steady and the lead varied.
Reversed: the lead came out too high, not too low.
Contradicted: paragraph 4 says the instrument itself was not the difficulty; the room was.
Wrong paragraph: melting and reworking is the problem with starting lead in paragraph 3, not the zircon result.

questions.stem: All of the following are mentioned in paragraph 5 as steps Patterson took to keep lead out of his laboratory EXCEPT:
choices: boiling the glassware in acid before use
keeping the room's air at a higher pressure than the hallway
storing the samples in sealed metal containers
redistilling water and reagents in quartz vessels
requiring anyone who entered to change into clean garments

proof.quote: boiled his glassware in acid
kept the air in the room at a slightly higher pressure than the hallway
redistilled his water and reagents in quartz vessels
required everyone who entered to change into clean garments

questions.why: Paragraph 5 lists sealing the walls, boiling glassware in acid, redistilling water and reagents in quartz, positive air pressure, and clean garments. Sealed metal containers appear nowhere, and metal is the last thing a lead-free lab would want near a sample.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 5: he boiled his glassware in acid.
Stated in paragraph 5: the room's air was kept at a slightly higher pressure than the hallway.
Stated in paragraph 5: he redistilled his water and reagents in quartz vessels.
Stated in paragraph 5: everyone who entered had to change into clean garments.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 5, the word 'blank' most nearly means
choices: a trial of the method with no sample in it
an empty space on a form where a result goes
a cartridge that fires without a bullet
a moment in which the memory fails
a sample so pure that it contains no lead

proof.quote: a run through the whole procedure with no sample at all, which reveals how much lead the method itself contributes

questions.why: Paragraph 5 defines the word in the same sentence: a run through the whole procedure with no sample at all, done to learn how much lead the method itself adds.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday meaning of the word, but the sentence describes a procedure, not a space on paper.
Another common meaning, with no connection to a laboratory procedure.
A figurative meaning that has nothing to do with the sentence.
Half right: the point of a blank is that there is no sample at all, not a very pure one.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the clean-laboratory work described in paragraph 5 is best described as
choices: amused
skeptical
indifferent
admiring
nostalgic

proof.quote: I think it was the most important thing he ever did

questions.why: Paragraph 5 calls the work slow and unglamorous and then says, I think it was the most important thing he ever did, because every later measurement rested on it. That is admiration.
distractorNotes: Wrong register: the author takes the drudgery seriously rather than finding it funny.
Reversed: the author endorses the work without reservation.
Too weak: the author makes a strong personal judgment about its importance.
Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 5 looks back fondly on a lost time; the work is praised for what it made possible.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, compared with the Canyon Diablo meteorite, a stony meteorite containing uranium would show
choices: lower ratios of lead-206 and lead-207 to lead-204
higher ratios of lead-206 and lead-207 to lead-204
the same lead ratios, since both formed at the same time
a larger amount of lead-204 relative to its uranium
a slope on the isochron plot that gives a younger age

proof.quote: had been accumulating radiogenic lead since they formed
Iron meteorites in particular contain almost no uranium, so whatever lead they hold has sat unchanged
the growing radiogenic isotopes, the ones born of decay

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says lead-206 and lead-207 grow by decay while lead-204 does not, paragraph 3 says the iron meteorite's lead has sat unchanged, and paragraph 6 says the stony meteorites had been accumulating radiogenic lead. So their ratios to lead-204 must be higher.
distractorNotes: Reversed: uranium decay adds lead-206 and lead-207, so the ratios rise, not fall.
Contradicted: paragraph 6 says the stony meteorites had been accumulating radiogenic lead, so their ratios moved while the iron meteorite's stayed put.
Reversed: lead-204 is not produced by decay, so it is the radiogenic isotopes, not lead-204, that are more abundant.
Confused: paragraph 6 says all the samples fall on one line with one slope; a single sample does not have its own age-giving slope.

questions.stem: According to the passage, lead from modern ocean sediment was included in the 1956 analysis in order to
choices: supply the primordial lead composition that the meteorites lacked
show that leaded gasoline had already reached the deep sea
correct the meteorite data for lead added by the laboratory
measure how much uranium the Earth's crust had lost over time
test whether the Earth and the meteorites were the same age

proof.quote: standing in for the Earth as a whole, fell on the same line, which meant the planet and the meteorites were the same age

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the ocean sediment stood in for the Earth as a whole and fell on the same line, which meant the planet and the meteorites were the same age.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the primordial lead came from the Canyon Diablo iron meteorite, not from the sediment.
Wrong paragraph: the seawater work on gasoline lead comes in paragraph 8, years later.
Wrong tool: the laboratory's added lead was measured with the blank in paragraph 5.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about uranium lost from the crust.

questions.stem: According to the passage, refiners added halogen compounds to leaded gasoline in order to
choices: stop engines from knocking at high compression
keep the lead particles from escaping into the air
carry the lead out of the engine through the exhaust
satisfy the Surgeon General's conditions for resuming sales
protect the catalytic converters in later cars

proof.quote: To keep lead from fouling the engine, refiners also blended in halogen compounds that carried it out of the tailpipe as fine particles

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says the halogen compounds were blended in to keep lead from fouling the engine, carrying it out of the tailpipe as fine particles.
distractorNotes: Wrong additive: stopping knock was the job of tetraethyl lead itself.
Reversed: the halogen compounds sent the lead out of the tailpipe as fine particles.
Outside the passage: no conditions from the Surgeon General are described.
Wrong paragraph and reversed: paragraph 10 says lead ruins a catalyst, so nothing in the fuel protected converters.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if the lead in the ocean had come mainly from natural sources on the sea floor, Patterson would have expected
choices: surface and deep water to hold no measurable lead at all
the surface water to hold far more lead than the deep water below it
the Greenland ice to show a steady decline in lead
the deep water to hold at least as much lead as the surface
the lead in the surface water to have come from leaded gasoline

proof.quote: a pattern that pointed to recent fallout from the air rather than to any natural source from below

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the surface excess pointed to fallout from the air rather than a natural source from below. A source on the sea floor would feed the deep water first, so the deep water should hold at least as much lead as the surface.
distractorNotes: Too extreme: a natural source would still put lead in the water; the question is where it would be concentrated.
Reversed: this is the pattern Patterson actually found, and it is what pointed away from the sea floor.
Wrong evidence: the Greenland ice is a separate record of the atmosphere, and the passage says it rose, not fell.
Reversed: gasoline fallout is the conclusion the surface excess supported, not what a sea-floor source would predict.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Patterson's 1965 paper argued that
choices: a typical modern body held about a hundred times the natural amount of lead
the body excretes nearly all of the lead that it absorbs from food and air
lead in Greenland ice had risen about two-hundredfold since ancient times
children with more lead in their baby teeth scored lower on tests of intelligence
ordinary people carried lead without any obvious signs of illness

proof.quote: the amount of lead in a typical modern body was not the natural amount but something like a hundred times higher

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the 1965 paper concluded that the lead in a typical modern body was not the natural amount but something like a hundred times higher.
distractorNotes: Wrong side of the debate: this was Kehoe's position in paragraph 9, not Patterson's.
Wrong year and wrong study: the Greenland ice result in paragraph 8 came in 1969.
Wrong person: this was Needleman's 1979 finding in paragraph 10.
Wrong side of the debate: paragraph 9 attributes this to Kehoe's thousands of measurements.

questions.stem: The author mentions Kehoe's thousands of measurements in paragraph 9 primarily to
choices: show that Kehoe had far more data than Patterson and was therefore more credible
prove that lead below a certain threshold causes no harm
explain why the Senate subcommittee rejected Patterson's testimony
illustrate the kind of blank that Patterson ran in his own laboratory
present the evidence that Patterson said rested on a mistaken baseline

proof.quote: he could point to thousands of measurements showing that ordinary people carried lead without obvious illness
every one of those measurements had been compared against the wrong baseline

questions.why: Paragraph 9 sets up Kehoe's thousands of measurements and then, in the very next sentence, gives Patterson's reply: every one of them had been compared against the wrong baseline. The measurements are there so the reply has something to answer.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author never says Kehoe was more credible; the next sentence undercuts his data.
Reversed: the author reports the threshold claim as Kehoe's view, not as proven, and paragraph 10 says Needleman found harm below it.
Outside the passage: the passage never says the subcommittee rejected Patterson.
Wrong paragraph: the blank belongs to paragraph 5 and has nothing to do with Kehoe.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the error the author describes in paragraph 8, confusing what is common with what is safe?
choices: A chemist discards a measurement because the blank came out higher than the sample itself
A town calls its water normal because its levels match those of nearby towns on the same river
A clinic flags a patient's blood pressure because it is higher than that of healthy adults
A factory reduces its emissions after a study finds harm at levels it had considered acceptable
A geologist estimates a rock's age from its lead without first measuring its starting composition

proof.quote: calling it normal confused what is common with what is safe
a judgment about what is normal is only as good as the baseline it is compared to

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says calling a contaminated level normal confuses what is common with what is safe, and paragraph 11 adds that a judgment about normal is only as good as its baseline. A town that judges its water by neighbors on the same contaminated river is using a contaminated baseline and calling the result normal.
distractorNotes: Reversed: throwing out a result when the blank is too high is the correct practice from paragraph 5, not the error.
Not the error: the patient is compared against healthy people, an uncontaminated baseline, and the high reading is flagged rather than called normal.
Not the error: this is the response to new evidence of harm, like the changes in paragraph 10.
A different mistake: skipping the starting composition is the catch in paragraph 3, not a confusion of common with safe.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following played a part in the removal of lead from gasoline between 1970 and 1996 EXCEPT:
choices: the Clean Air Act of 1970
catalytic converters on new cars
the Surgeon General's conference
Needleman's study of children's teeth
the Clean Air Act amendments of 1990

proof.quote: The Clean Air Act of 1970 gave the new Environmental Protection Agency authority over fuel additives
because lead ruins a catalyst, those cars required unleaded fuel
children with more lead in their shed baby teeth scored lower on tests of intelligence and attention
under amendments passed in 1990 the sale of leaded gasoline for road vehicles ended
the additive returned to the market in 1926

questions.why: Paragraph 10 names the 1970 act, the catalytic converters, Needleman's teeth study, and the 1990 amendments as parts of the phase-out. The Surgeon General's conference belongs to paragraph 7 and the 1920s, and it ended with the additive returning to the market.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 10: the 1970 act gave the new agency authority over fuel additives.
Stated in paragraph 10: lead ruins a catalyst, so the new cars needed unleaded fuel.
Stated in paragraph 10: Needleman's 1979 study found harm at levels once called safe.
Stated in paragraph 10: the 1990 amendments ended sales for road vehicles in 1996.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the sale of leaded gasoline for road vehicles in the United States ended
choices: at the start of 1996, a few weeks after Patterson's death
in 1985, when the EPA cut the permitted lead content by ninety percent
in 1975, when catalytic converters became standard on new cars
in 1973, when the EPA first ordered a gradual reduction
in 1990, when Congress passed amendments to the Clean Air Act

proof.quote: the sale of leaded gasoline for road vehicles ended on the first day of 1996
Patterson died in December 1995, a few weeks before the ban took full effect.

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says the sale ended on the first day of 1996 and that Patterson died in December 1995, a few weeks before the ban took full effect.
distractorNotes: Wrong step: 1985 was a steep cut in the allowed amount, not the end of sales.
Wrong step: 1975 brought the converters and unleaded pumps, but leaded fuel was still sold.
Wrong step: 1973 was the start of a gradual reduction, not the end.
Half right: the 1990 amendments ordered the end, but the passage says it took effect in 1996.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Patterson's age for the Earth was wrong by less than one percent, which proves that his clean-room methods were unnecessary
Leaded gasoline was banned in the United States mainly because it ruined the catalytic converters on new cars
Robert Kehoe's threshold theory was correct for adults but failed to account for the vulnerability of children
The rigorous measurement Patterson developed to date the Earth also exposed how much lead humans had added to the environment
Meteorites are the only reliable source of primordial lead, so the age of the Earth can never be measured from terrestrial rocks

proof.quote: clearing it away changed his career and eventually the air of the whole country
Patterson's two careers used one tool.
The same discipline that let him trust a few billionths of a gram of lead from a meteorite let him see the lead in seawater

questions.why: Paragraph 1 promises that clearing lead from the lab changed both Patterson's career and the country's air, and paragraph 11 closes by saying his two careers used one tool. The passage is about one habit of measurement that answered two questions.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the author says every later measurement rested on the clean-room work, and the near-accuracy is presented as its reward.
Too narrow: the converters are one step among several in paragraph 10, and the passage is about far more than the ban.
Outside the passage: the author never endorses Kehoe's threshold for anyone, and paragraph 10 presents evidence against it.
Too extreme and too narrow: this is one step in paragraph 3, and the passage never says never.
